paper_title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.

Introduction Monocular real-time human mesh recovery (HMR) is long-standing goal in computer vision, with applications tele-rehabilitation [39], workplace erin robotics [10], gonomics [13, 21], AR/VR [12, 27], exergames [45], and 3D animation [37]. Since 2023, most smartphones include neural processing unit (NPU), which is formidable opportunity for local real-time inference, fostering privacy, low energy consumption and ease of use. with remarkable robustness [29, 34, 44], but they are built for GPUs: SAM 3D Body [44] takes 416 ms per person on desktop GPU in its own release and does not run on phones NPU at all. NLF [34] is the fastest state-of-the-art model on desktop GPU (1.52 ms per person for the smallest variant), but is not tailored for real-time mobile inference (67.97 ms per person on Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU). sections.title: Recent models recover a body mesh from a single image
sections.content: 1In this context, real-time means latency lower than 33 ms, 30 fps 1 accuracy (cf. Tab. 2 and Fig. 1). We present InstantHMR, family of single-image HMR models designed for phones. InstantHMR regresses the parameters of the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) [7] with an efficient convolutional backbone [46] and small transformer decoder. It is trained on the publicly released annotations of SAM 3D Bodys training set. On Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, InstantHMR-M recovers 6,890-vertex mesh in 5.5 ms per person, faster than every method we measure and 12 and 23 faster than NLF-S and NLF-L, the only phone-compatible methods that outperform ours in accuracy (cf. Fig. 1 and Tab. 1). Published numbers on EMDB [15] and 3DPW [40] are produced under different person boxes, focal lengths, joint sets and conversions between body models, and these choices move single model by several millimetres (supplementary material), as much as the gaps between methods. We therefore re-evaluate eleven methods under one protocol, matched to the closest MHRbased competitors, and report for each how closely we reproduce its paper. In summary, our contributions are: InstantHMR, family of four MHR regressors (nano to medium) that trace one accuracy/latency curve, trained only on released annotations; InstantHMR-M runs in real time on phone NPU at 48.8 mm PA-MPJPE on EMDB1, 40.0 mm on 3DPW and 41.7 mm on RICH. matched evaluation protocol with Metas official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, under which eleven competitors are re-scored, each with reproduction verdict against its own paper. Latency on eight targets, from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs and two phone CPUs, measured the same way for every method. The code (Apache-2.0) and the models (for noncommercial use) are available at https://github. com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR. We also provide commercially safe variant of the medium model (InstantHMR-M-C) trained on smaller corpus of images with permissive license (cf. Tab. 3). 2. Related work Parametric body models. Most HMR methods do not predict mesh directly, but the parameters of parametric body model that maps few pose and shape coefficients to skinned mesh. SMPL [25] is by far the most used, with 6,890-vertex mesh, 24 joints and shape space learned from 3D scans. SMPL-H [32] adds articulated hands, and SMPL-X [30] adds both hands and an expressive face. More recently, Meta released the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) [7], which decouples the skeleton from the body shape. Unlike SMPL, Anny [3] does not learn its shape space from 3D scans. Its shape is set by interpretable parameters such as age, height and weight, built on the opensource MakeHuman software and calibrated on WHO population statistics, so that single model spans bodies from infants to elders. SOMA [33] goes one step further and maps SMPL, SMPL-X, MHR and Anny to single canonical mesh and skeleton. These models differ in topology, skeleton and units, so comparing methods that predict different models requires converting between them, which is key part of our protocol (Sec. 4). InstantHMR predicts in MHR parametric space. Human mesh recovery from single image. Historically, HMR [14] consists in regressing SMPL parameters from single image. HMR2.0 [8] scales this formulation with ViT backbone and large pseudo-labelled data, TokenHMR [6] predicts the pose as discrete tokens, CLIFF [23] conditions the regressor on the location of the person in the full frame, and CameraHMR [29] adds camera-aware head trained with estimated focal lengths. HybrIK [19] recovers the rotations from 3D keypoints with analytical inverse kinematics, and NLF [34] predicts any body point as continuous field, which allows training single model on annotations from different skeletons and meshes. SMPLer-X [4] and Multi-HMR [2] regress the expressive SMPL-X model, for one person or for many at once, and the authors of Anny show that Multi-HMR model trained on synthetic Anny images matches its scanbased counterparts [3]. SAM 3D Body [44] moves to MHR with promptable DINOv3-based architecture trained on large human-annotated corpus, and Fast SAM 3D Body [43] accelerates it by up to 10.9 without retraining. NVIDIAs GEM-X [28] also builds on DINOv3 and predicts SOMA. It provides single-image model, and video model that we discuss in the next paragraph. These recent models are remarkably robust, but they are built for GPUs. InstantHMR predicts in MHR parametric space, with an architecture tailored to phone inference. Human mesh recovery from video. Video methods use the temporal information to recover smoother and more accurate motion, often in world coordinates. WHAM [38] lifts sequences of 2D keypoints to 3D, fuses them with the features of pretrained single-image encoder, and estimates the global trajectory with recurrent networks that only look at past frames, so it runs online. TRAM [41] and GVHMR [36] recover the global trajectory and motion of people from whole sequences, GEM [20] unifies motion estimation and generation in single diffusion-based model, and the video model of GEM-X [28] follows the motion over the sequence from the features of its single-image model and 2D keypoints. FastHMR [26] accelerates ViT regressor by merging tokens and layers, then denoises the pose over 243-frame clips with diffusion decoder, reaching 103150 FPS on an RTX 3090. 2 Figure 2. InstantHMR. 288 px crop around the person goes through convolutional HGNetV2 encoder (shown: the first principal component of its second-stage features, 36 36, contrast-stretched) down to 9 9 image tokens. 4-layer transformer decoder refines 71 learned queries (one for the body, one per keypoint) by attention among themselves and to the image tokens; the boxs position in the full frame (two viewing angles and the size over the focal length) is embedded and added to every query. The body query feeds the MHR and camera heads, from which the rigs forward kinematics (FK) gives the posed mesh; each keypoint query feeds SimCC head that classifies its and over 96 bins (shown over the crop: for each keypoint, the product of its two distributions). Every visual is the real output of InstantHMR-M on 3DPW test frame [40]. InstantHMR-M has 32.2 parameters: 13.6 in the backbone, 16.8 in the decoder, and 1.8 in the projections, queries and heads. Efficient and on-device recovery. Many applications such as AR/VR, tele-rehabilitation or the teleoperation of robots, need low latency and not only high throughput: the pose of frame must be available while that frame is captured. Most video methods induce latency, since an output that depends on future frames has to wait for them: FastHMR waits for up to 242 later frames, about 8 at 30 FPS. Online methods such as WHAM avoid this wait, but still need per-frame image model: the 200 FPS reported for WHAM exclude its ViTPose keypoint detector and its pretrained image encoder [38]. This study therefore focuses on the single-image model, which estimates the current frame from that frame alone and is the per-frame building block of online video methods such as WHAM. Among single-image methods, efficient HMR has mostly targeted GPUs, e.g. Seeing Machines reports 5.515.8 ms on an NVIDIA Jetson Thor robotics module [35]. On phones, BlazePose GHUM Holistic [9] estimates 3D landmarks in real time and lifts them to body model, but is not evaluated on standard mesh benchmark. The closest work to ours is MeshPose [18], which localises low-poly SMPL mesh with DensePose-style supervision and runs at 97153 FPS on an iPhone 12, depending on the backbone; we evaluate its released model in Sec. 5. Evaluation protocols. 3DPW [40], EMDB [15] and RICH [11] are the standard in-the-wild benchmarks, but papers evaluate on them in different ways. They differ in the person boxes (ground truth or detections), the focal length (calibrated or fixed field of view), and, for methods that do not output SMPL, the conversion to SMPL. For instance, SAM 3D Body converts MHR to SMPL with Metas iterative fitter, Fast SAM 3D Body replaces that fitter with learned network, and GEM-X releases its own datasetspecific projectors. Each of these choices moves single model by several millimetres, so we fix one protocol, the one of the closest MHR-based competitors, and re-run every method under it (Sec. 4). 3. InstantHMR InstantHMR takes square crop of the person, R2882883, and the position of that crop in the full image, R3 (defined in Sec. 3.1). It returns three outputs  (Fig. 2)  . The first is the persons MHR parameters: the rig parameters θ R204, which hold the root translation and rotation, 130 joint parameters and 68 bone scales, and the identity coefficients β R45, which shape the body surface. The second is, for each of the 70 2D keypoints, two probability distributions over 96 bins, one for its and one for its coordinate, [0, 1]70296 (SimCC [22]). Their expectations give the 2D keypoints R702, in crop coordinates. The third is the camera translation R3, which places the body in the camera frame. The MHR rig then turns (θ, β) into the posed mesh = M(θ, β) R6,8903 and its 70 3D keypoints R703, which are in camera coordinates once translated by t. is farthest-point sub3 set of MHRs 18,439-vertex mesh, with as many vertices as SMPL, so that every methods latency is measured up to mesh of the same size. Every design choice serves one constraint: the whole network must compile to phone NPU, in fp16, with no operator falling back to the CPU. The mathematical details of this section, the equations of the network and of the losses, are given in the supplementary material. 3.1. Network HGNetV2 Backbone. convolutional HGNetV2 [46] backbone E, pretrained on ImageNet, turns the 288 288 crop into 9 9 grid of features. linear layer projects them to = 512 channels, and fixed 2D sine-cosine positional embedding is added, which gives the 81 image tokens = E(I) R81d. Convolutions, unlike the attention of ViT backbone, map directly onto the operators phone NPUs accelerate. The four sizes of InstantHMR differ only in the backbone (B0, B1, B2, B4 for nano, tiny, small, medium), and have 20.0, 20.3, 24.4 and 32.2 parameters. The decoder and the heads are the same in every size, and the decoder alone holds 16.8 of these parameters. CLIFF conditioning. crop alone does not determine where the person is in 3D: the same crop could come from the centre or the edge of wide-angle image. As in CLIFF [23], the network therefore receives the position of the crop in the full image, but expressed through the focal length rather than the image size, so that it keeps one meaning across cameras. For box of centre (bx, by) and size bw bh in an image of size H, holds the two viewing angles of the box centre, arctan((bx W/2)/f ) and arctan((by H/2)/f ), and the box size max(bw, bh)/f . two-layer MLP ϕ embeds it into ϕ(c) Rd. At deployment, without calibration, defaults to 1.05 the image diagonal. 71 learned queries R71d, Transformer Decoder. one for the body and one per 2D keypoint, receive the position embedding ϕ(c), added to every query. 4-layer prenorm transformer decoder [5] (8 heads) then lets them attend to each other and to the image tokens F, and outputs one feature zi Rd per query. The feature z0 comes from the body query, and z1, . . . , z70 from the keypoint queries. Decoder Heads. Three heads read the decoder output. The SimCC head h2D, two-layer MLP shared by all keypoints, turns each keypoint query into its two distributions, Pk = h2D(zk), whose expectations over the bin centres give the 2D keypoint xk. Classifying the coordinates rather than regressing them keeps the image evidence of every joint in the decoder. The camera head hcam, linear layer, predicts the camera translation from the body query, = hcam(z0). The MHR head hMHR predicts the body from the same query, (θ, β) = hMHR(z0). It is two-layer head in SAM 3D Bodys continuous parameterisation: the root rotation as 6D vector [47], the body pose in its continuous form, the identity coefficients β, 28 bone-scale principal components and two hand blocks, which are decoded into the rig parameters θ. The root translation is fixed to zero (the person is placed by the camera translation), and the bone-scale coefficients and the six limb-length parameters are bounded to the range seen in training. Without these bounds, the scales enter the rigs forward kinematics multiplicatively along each limb, and single large prediction can produce skeleton hundreds of metres tall that diverges the training. The 3D keypoints are not regressed: they are read from the posed rig through its own forward kinematics, so 3D keypoints and mesh can never disagree. 3.2. Training Dataset. InstantHMR is trained on the human-annotated MHR fits that Meta released with SAM 3D Body [44], over the images of five of its sources: SA-1B [17], AI Challenger [42], Harmony4D [16], COCO [24] and MPII [1], 4.2 person crops in total, sampled at 43 / 26 / 14 / 13 / 4 %. No 3DPW or EMDB images are used. The labels are the datasets annotations, not the predictions of teacher model, so the student is not capped at teachers accuracy. Losses. The training loss is weighted sum of eleven terms, which fall into three groups. The first group compares the predicted MHR parameters with the annotated ones: the joint parameters, the root rotation, the bone scales, the identity coefficients and the camera translation. The second group compares the geometry that the rig produces from these parameters: the 70 3D keypoints, 595 vertices spread over the mesh, and the 127 joints of the skeleton. As in NLF [34], the keypoint and vertex errors are plain Euclidean distances, not squared ones, so that few bad samples do not dominate the gradient. The vertex term matters for shape: the identity coefficients β move the mesh but not the skeleton, so without it they receive no geometric gradient at all. The third group supervises the image side: the SimCC cross-entropy against Gaussian label centred on each annotated keypoint, distance on the 2D keypoints x, and reprojection term that projects the 3D keypoints with the predicted translation and the calibrated camera, and compares them with the annotated 2D keypoints. The 40 finger keypoints weigh 0.2 in the 3D and reprojection terms, and the terms that go through the rig are ramped up over the first 2,000 steps. We tuned the weights of the eleven terms empirically, with single-batch overfitting tests and by balancing the measured gradient norm of each term; the equations and the weights are given in the supplementary material. 4 Accuracy (mm) Latency per person (ms) EMDBRTX 4070 CPU Phone NPU (fp16) Phone CPU (fp32)

Training Recipe and Deployment. Each model is trained for 600 epochs of 400 samples, batch 256 on four GPUs, with AdamW and one-cycle learning-rate schedule peaking at 6 104. Each training crop is either the standard crop (probability 0.75) or one of three other framings cut from the full image (zoomed out, zoomed in, shifted), with synthetic occlusion. This mix is the largest single gain we measured (Tab. 4): against training on the standard crop alone, it improves EMDB-1 PA-MPJPE by 10.0 mm (58.8 to 48.8) and 3DPW by 2.7 mm, more than an even or uniform mix of the framings. The 288 px input is the second: at every backbone size, it improves EMDB-1 PA-MPJPE by 4.45.5 mm over 224 px (Tab. 4 for the medium backbone, the supplementary material for the others). 4. Evaluation protocol How method is scored on 3DPW and EMDB moves its error by several millimetres, as much as the gaps between methods. The supplementary material shows this for InstantHMR-M alone: on EMDB-1, the choice of person boxes, focal length and body-model conversion moves its PA-MPJPE between 46.9 and 50.1 mm, and learned conversion network [43] raises it to 65.9 mm. Picking the most favourable setting per benchmark would be protocol shopping. Our protocol is not the most favourable one for us: detector boxes score InstantHMR-M 1.9 mm better than the ground-truth boxes we report. We fix one protocol before scoring our models under it: the one of our closest competitors, the MHR-based SAM 3D Body and Fast SAM 3D Body, and score every method under it. The network exports to single ONNX graph, which runs in fp16 on the S23 NPU with all of its 1,607 layers on the NPU. For the latency we report, the graph also includes the rigs forward kinematics and linear blend skinning up to the posed mesh V. Settings. Every method is scored on the same frames, with the same person boxes and the same camera. The person boxes are the ones the benchmarks provide: EMDB ships one per frame, and for 3DPW, which ships none, we take the extent of the annotated 2D keypoints enlarged by 20 %. Reproduction. We run each competitor from its released code and weights, with its own crop and preprocessing, and compare our score with the one printed in its paper, on the joint set of that paper. We call method reproduced when the two PA-MPJPE differ by less than 1 mm. NLF-S and TokenHMR reproduce on both benchmarks, and CameraHMR on 3DPW. NLF-L scores 1.92.2 mm better than its paper, and SAM 3D Body, Fast SAM 3D Body, HybrIK, and CameraHMR on EMDB-1 score 1.34.5 mm worse. On RICH, CameraHMR reproduces its published number (0.4 mm better), SAM 3D Body scores 2.6 mm worse and Fast SAM 3D Body 1.7 mm better than their papers. HMR2.0b scores 9.9 mm worse than the run of it reported by SAM 3D Body, whose crop is not stated, while our harness reproduces HMR2.0b on EMDB-1 within 0.4 mm. Such gaps can come from settings that paper does not fully specify, and we do not claim that any published number is wrong. Latency. Latency is the models time per person crop at batch 1, from the crop to posed mesh of up to 6,890 vertices; detection and cropping are excluded for every method. Desktop timings are medians over interleaved rounds, so background load affects all methods alike. Phone timings use Qualcomm AI Hub [31] on physical devices, the median of three jobs. Only complete methods are timed: method that does not export whole is timed in its own release (HybrIK, SAM 3D Body, Fast SAM 3D Body), and partial timings are left to the supplementary material. 5. Experiments We evaluate on EMDB-1 [15], 3DPW test [40] and RICH test [11] under the protocol of Sec. 4. None of the three benchmarks images are in InstantHMRs training data; four competitors trained on 3DPW-train (marked ), and three on RICH (), which makes EMDB-1 the fairer of the three. Speed (Tab. 1). On the Galaxy S23 NPU, InstantHMR-M takes 5.49 ms per person, and 4.01 ms on the S24. Only one other method is real time on the phone: SMPLer-X-S32, at 11.12 ms, but 22 mm less accurate on EMDB-1. Every ViTH and DINOv3-based method (CameraHMR, TokenHMR, HMR2.0, SAM 3D Body, Fast SAM 3D Body) fails to run on either phone NPU, for lack of memory or because the compiled model fails. On the desktop GPU, InstantHMRM takes 0.98 ms with TensorRT, the fastest of all methods (nano: 0.70 ms). Why InstantHMR is fast on the NPU. On the S23s CPU, InstantHMR-M (93 ms) and NLF-S (103 ms) are close, and on the desktop GPU they are 1.6 apart, but on the NPU NLF-S is 12 slower. Both models run entirely on the NPU (807 of 807 layers for NLF-S, 1,607 of 1,607 for InstantHMR-M), so the gap does not come from layers falling back to the CPU: it comes from how each model produces the mesh. NLF estimates each vertex as separate query point with its own 8 8 8 heatmap, whose score-weighted average gives the vertex position. For 6,890 vertices, most of the work is moving and summing tensors of 6,890 512 values, which an NPU, built for convolutions and matrix products, does slowly: gathers, reductions, transposes, reshapes and softmaxes take 71% of NLF-Ss NPU time, its convolutions under 2%. With 1,048 query 7 points instead of 6,890, the same network runs in 8.1 ms. InstantHMR instead regresses the 204 MHR parameters once per person, with convolutional backbone and small decoder, operators the NPU is designed for; the mesh then follows from the rigs forward kinematics and skinning, fixed weighted sum whose cost does not depend on the network. Accuracy (Tab. 2). Among the methods that run on InstantHMR-M is 2025 mm more accurate phone, than SMPLer-X, MeshPose, HybrIK and Multi-HMR on EMDB-1 (PA-MPJPE), and 915 mm on 3DPW. MeshPose, the closest phone-oriented work, is released only with its HRNet-32 backbone, which scores 73.7 mm on EMDB-1 and 49.7 mm on 3DPW against 48.8 and 40.0 mm for InstantHMR-M; its paper reports its phone-sized variants, which are not released, 23 mm behind that model on 3DPW2. On hard poses, the gap can be much larger than these averages  (Fig. 3)  . Only NLF is more accurate, at 12 (NLF-S) and 23 (NLF-L) the phone latency; on 3DPW, InstantHMR-M is within 0.6 mm of NLFS. Without the phone constraint, Fast SAM 3D Body and SAM 3D Body remain the most accurate, 810 mm better than InstantHMR-M on EMDB-1, at 130416 ms per person on desktop GPU. With detector boxes in place of the ground-truth ones (InstantHMR-M + det.), InstantHMR-M improves to 46.9 mm on EMDB-1 and 39.3 mm on 3DPW, the setting NLF is evaluated in. RICH shows the same picture: InstantHMR-M (41.7 mm) is 1828 mm more accurate than HybrIK, Multi-HMR and SMPLer-X, which is trained on RICH. Among the methods that run on phone, only NLF, also trained on RICH, is more accurate; and CameraHMR, SAM 3D Body and Fast SAM 3D Body are 8 10 mm better than InstantHMR-M. The family (Tab. 3). From nano to medium, EMDB1 PA-MPJPE improves from 61.7 to 48.8 mm (53.5 to 41.7 mm on RICH), while the S23 NPU latency only grows from 4.60 to 5.49 ms: on the phone NPU, the latency barely depends on the backbone size, so medium is the natural choice. On the S23 CPU, it is different story, the latency triples from nano to medium (31.5 to 93.0 ms), and nano is the only size that runs in real time there. On phones without usable NPU, the smaller sizes are therefore worth the accuracy they lose. Training on commercially usable images only (Harmony4D and COCO, M-C) costs 23 mm on EMDB-1, with 0.5 of the 4.2 training crops: the training images matter more than any architectural change we tried. 2MeshPose-S / -XS, as published [18]: 3DPW PA-MPJPE 48.97 / 49.71 mm on 14 LSP joints from the authors unreleased landmarker; 99 / 153 FPS on an iPhone 12 with CoreML. Weights not released; not comparable with our rows. The input-size pair uses an earlier recipe (hence 49.8, not 48.8 mm); other backbones in the supplementary material. 6. Limitations and conclusion Limitations. InstantHMR has no dedicated hand encoder or decoder. The hands are read from the same 288 288 crop of the whole person and the same 9 9 image tokens as the rest of the body, where hand covers only few pixels. SAM 3D Body, in contrast, refines the hands with second decoder that runs on crops around each hand. Adding light hand branch, without losing the real-time latency on the phone NPU, is left for future work. All our phone measurements are on Android phones with Qualcomm NPUs (Galaxy S23 and S24). We did not evaluate InstantHMR on Apple silicon (the Neural Engine of iPhones, through Core ML), which is also left for future work. InstantHMR estimates each frame on its own, and we report no temporal metric (jitter or acceleration error), although the applications we target are sensitive to it; evaluating it, with and without the 1 Euro filter of our released demo, is future work. Finally, InstantHMR is trained on the released annotations of the SAM 3D Body dataset, but many of its images, such as those of SA-1B and AI Challenger, may only be used for research. For this reason, the nano, tiny, small and medium models are released for research use only. InstantHMR-M-C, trained only on commercially usable images (Harmony4D and COCO), can be used in commercial products, but it is much less accurate: 72.2 mm PAMPJPE on EMDB-1 against 48.8 mm for InstantHMR-M. Closing this gap requires more training images with permissive licences, real or synthetic. Conclusion. We presented InstantHMR, family of single-image MHR regressors built for phone NPUs. On the Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, InstantHMR-M recovers 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.49 ms per person, at 48.8 mm PA-MPJPE on EMDB-1, 40.0 mm on 3DPW and 41.7 mm on RICH. It is the most accurate method that runs in real time on the phone; the two methods that are more accurate 8 and also run on phone NPU, NLF-S and NLF-L, are 12 and 23 slower there. To make these comparisons fair, we re-evaluated eleven methods under one protocol, matched to the closest MHR-based competitors, and reported how closely each reproduces its paper. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpadstudio/InstantHMR.

sections.content: This work was granted access to the HPC resources of IDRIS under the allocation AD011017116 made by GENCI. We thank Meta for releasing the annotations of the SAM 3D Body dataset and the MHR body model.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: We used Claude Code (Anthropic), an LLM-based coding assistant, to write and run evaluation code under our direction (competitor reproduction, scoring, latency meato surement, and the generation of tables and figures), search the literature, and to draft and edit text. The model, its training and the experimental design are ours; we reviewed all code, verified every source and revised all text, and every number comes from saved result files.
